sentences_with_numbers: 5 failure modes that kill AI projects, a rescue-vs-rebuild decision framework, and realistic recovery costs.
Book a rescue diagnostic — free 30-min consultation
The 5 failure modes behind almost every stalled AI project
Mode 1: solved the wrong problem.
Mode 2: the data wasn't ready.
Mode 3: no owner.
Mode 4: demo-grade build.
Mode 5: no success metric.
Plan for 4–8 weeks at 30–50% of the original budget.
Weeks 1–2 are a forensic audit.
Weeks 3–6 are the fix itself.
Weeks 7–8 are handover: monitoring dashboards, a trained internal owner, and a runbook for when things break.
Indicative numbers for this type of work: our indicative range for a diagnostic audit is €2,500–5,000 depending on system complexity, and is deductible from the rescue if you proceed.
Budget €8,000–25,000 for a rescue of this scope.

The right comparison is not 'that's expensive' but three other figures: the sunk cost of the original project (often €20–60k), the ongoing monthly cost of the process still being done manually, and the cost of doing nothing while competitors automate.
A useful mental rule: if the rescued system would save or earn more than €1,500/month, a mid-range rescue pays for itself within a year.

An illustrative scenario — a composite example, not a specific client: a distribution company had spent around €40,000 on an AI order-processing system that performed well in testing but failed on real orders, and was abandoned within two months of launch.
In this illustrative scenario the finished system processes roughly 70% of incoming orders untouched, with the remainder routed to a human queue with the AI's draft already attached.
A diagnostic audit answers the question definitively within 1–2 weeks, before you commit to anything larger.
As a planning assumption, 30–50% of the original project budget, with the diagnostic audit (€2,500–5,000) fixed in advance and deducted if you proceed.
A conversion audit checklist, the 7 most common causes, and realistic fixes.
The 7 conversion killers we find in audits
Step 1: export 50 recent conversations.
A healthy bot converts 20–30% of engaged conversations into a next step; most broken ones are under 5%.
Step 2: categorize what people actually ask.
Expect 5–8 topics to cover 80% of volume.
Step 3: check how the bot answers those top topics — with your specifics (your prices, your process, your timelines) or with generic filler text.
Step 4: test the failure path.
Step 5: check what happens after the chat.

An illustrative scenario — a composite example, not a specific client: a professional services firm had a chatbot handling roughly 400 conversations a month and producing a handful of leads — around 3 in a typical month, a conversion rate under 1%.

In this illustrative scenario, conversion moves to the 15–25% range — the same traffic simply starts producing what it should have produced all along, on the order of dozens of qualified leads per month instead of a few.
Plan for 3–5 weeks including measurement setup, so you can prove the improvement with before/after numbers.
On high-intent traffic, 15–25% conversation-to-lead is a realistic target range to design for.
Sustained rates under 5% mean something structural is broken.
See how we deliver in 6-week cycles
It runs at 3am when nobody is watching.
Weeks 1–2: gap assessment against the seven-point checklist, producing a scoped production plan with fixed costs.
Weeks 3–8: close the gaps — in practice this concentrates on hardening the data pipeline, building the real integration, and setting up the human review workflow.
Weeks 8–12: staged rollout, and this staging matters more than any technology decision.
Plan on €10,000–20,000 to turn a €15,000 pilot into a dependable production system — the range depends mainly on how messy the data reality is and how many systems need connecting.
4–8 weeks is enough to prove value on a well-scoped pilot.
If a pilot has been 'almost ready' for 6+ months, it isn't validating anymore — it's stuck.
The 4 root causes of wrong answers
Cause 1: the bot can't find the right information.
Cause 2: no grounding requirement.
Cause 3: vague questions get confident answers.
The bot never asks clarifying questions and was never given instructions to say 'I don't know, let me connect you to a person.' Cause 4: nobody measures accuracy.
Step 1: assemble 50–100 real questions with known correct answers.
Step 2: run the test set through the bot and score every answer as right, wrong, or partial.
Step 3: fix by error category.
Step 4: re-test until you reach target.
For bounded business domains — your products, your services, your policies — accuracy of 95% or higher is an achievable engineering target, not an aspiration.
Step 5: keep the test set forever and re-run it after every change to content, prompts, or model.
Can AI chatbots be 100% accurate?
No system is 100%.
But for bounded business domains, 95%+ accuracy with clean human handover for the remainder is achievable — and that combination is operationally excellent.
Build a test set of 50–100 real questions with known correct answers and score the bot against it.
The 4 places AI money leaks
Leak 1: overlapping subscriptions.
Leak 2: per-seat pricing on ghost seats — you're paying for 25 seats, the usage dashboard shows 7 active humans.
Leak 3: unmonitored API usage.
Leak 4: enterprise tiers bought for a feature that was never switched on.
Step 1: pull every AI-related charge from accounting — tool subscriptions, API invoices, per-seat licenses.
Step 2: for each line item, answer four questions: who uses it, for which process, how often, and what happens if it disappears tomorrow.
Step 3: open the usage dashboards.
Step 4: for usage-based spend, identify the top three consumption sources.
Step 5: mark every line keep, consolidate, downgrade, or kill.
In an illustrative audit of this kind, 30–50% of current spend is identified as recoverable — before anything changes about how the work actually gets done.
Breakeven versus stacked subscriptions arrives at around 12–24 months.

Illustrative reference ranges for an SME: uncontrolled sprawl totals in the region of €1,000–5,000 per month across tools, seats, and usage.
A consolidated stack — one or two subscriptions plus one or two purpose-built automations with managed API usage — runs in the region of €300–800 per month ongoing, with better outcomes attached.
The purpose-built pieces carry a one-time build cost (€8,000–25,000 depending on scope), which is where the 12–24 month breakeven comes from.
First, if someone proposes building custom AI while you're at €300/month in effective subscriptions, that's usually the wrong advice — custom earns its cost at volume.
Second, if you're at €3,000/month of sprawl with no measurable outcome, the problem isn't the amount — it's that you can't name what any of it does.
When per-transaction pricing or several overlapping subscriptions exceed the amortized build cost — typically at 12–24 months of the subscription alternative.
Step 1: Secure your assets before anything else
Step 2: Get an independent technical assessment
A competent independent assessment takes one to two weeks and costs in the region of €2,000–5,000.
Step 3: Decide — finish, fix, or walk away
A €40,000 spend doesn't make a bad project worth €20,000 more.

The patterns that predict failure: payments decoupled from demonstrable progress; no acceptance criteria ('working AI' is not a criterion — 'correctly processes 95% of this test set' is); code you cannot see until the end; and confidence instead of cadence — 'trust us' instead of a demo every two weeks.
Signal 1: containment below 30% — most conversations either escalate to a human anyway or simply die, meaning the bot adds friction without resolving anything.
Signal 2: 'human, agent, person' are among the most-typed phrases in your transcripts — visitors have learned the bot is a tollbooth to pass, not help to receive.
Signal 3: every new question type requires someone to manually build a new branch, so coverage improvement has stopped; the tree you have is the tree you'll die with.
Signal 4: maintenance has become its own part-time job — updating flows, fixing broken branches, chasing the tool's quirks.
Weeks 1–2: mine your transcripts.
This produces your top 20–30 intents with real phrasing — the new system's foundation.
Weeks 3–4: build the AI system against your knowledge base, wire the integrations, and configure human handover so escalations carry full context.
Week 5: parallel running — the AI goes live alongside the legacy bot, handling conversations while the old system remains as fallback.
Week 6: cutover, once the numbers hold.

Illustrative trajectory when a rule-based bot is replaced by a properly grounded AI system: containment moves from the roughly 30% ceiling of decision trees to the 70–85% range, because understanding free text is the entire point of the new architecture.
Running costs for the AI layer land in the region of €100–500 per month depending on conversation volume — usually offset before anything else by reduced maintenance effort alone.
Plan for 5–6 weeks including a parallel-running phase.
Usage runs in the region of €100–500/month depending on volume.
The 3 integration patterns, explained plainly

Plan for 4–8 weeks for a single well-defined workflow, from kickoff to production, including testing and staged rollout with human review.
How to measure it properly, when to re-prompt vs retrain, and how to reach 95%+ on business tasks.
Step 1: Build a test set from reality, not imagination

A test set is 50–100 real inputs your AI actually faces — genuine customer questions, actual documents you process, real orders — each paired with the verified correct output, confirmed by a human expert on your team.
Step 2: Score it, and categorize every error
With it, you fix the two categories that account for 80% of errors and watch the number move.
Step 3: The escalation ladder — cheapest fix first
For bounded business tasks — answering from your documents, extracting from your standard forms, classifying your request types — accuracy of 95% and above is an engineering target, not a hope.
'95% with graceful handover' outperforms '99% with silent failure' in every real-world measure, because trust is won or lost on how a system fails, not on how often.
The full test set after every change to the system; light random sampling (5–10 items weekly) continuously in production, to catch drift.
Is 95% accuracy enough to automate a process?
Depends what's at stake — but 95% with human review of low-confidence cases is usually the right operating point.
Design the handover; 100% doesn't exist.
'It saves €6,400 a month against €2,100 in costs, here's the one-pager' survives and compounds.

Count all of it: subscriptions and usage fees; the amortized build cost (a €24,000 build is €1,000/month over two years, and should appear as such); the internal hours spent managing, correcting, and feeding the system; and — the line item nobody includes — the cost of its residual errors, the human review time and the occasional mistake that gets through.
Illustrative worked example: a document-processing system saves roughly 180 hours a month against €6,300 of loaded labor cost; its all-in costs are €1,800 monthly.
Net €4,500 a month, honestly counted — payback inside five months.

Our planning model for well-chosen automation assumes payback within 6–12 months and 200–400% annual ROI thereafter — an illustration to reason with, not a promise — but only measured projects ever find out which side of that they're on.
Most AI marketing runs on vague claims — ‘transformative’, ‘game-changing’, ‘10x’.
